design_detail: Conceptual narrative review in the journal's 'Fundamental concepts in genetics' series by three quantitative geneticists: definitions of broad- and narrow-sense heritability as ratios of variances (Box 1), common misconceptions (Box 2), history of the term (Box 3), the heritability of IQ (Box 4), heritability of all-or-none traits on the observed and liability scales (Box 5), heritability of new phenotypes (Box 6), estimation designs and their assumptions, why heritability changes, effects of selection and inbreeding, and marker-based estimation. Examples come from livestock, plants, insects, wild animals and human height, IQ, schizophrenia and major depression. No search strategy and no appraisal of the cited studies. No drug-use or addiction phenotype is discussed anywhere in the review.
can_establish: What heritability means as a technical term (a ratio of variances in a particular population for a measurement taken at a particular time or age), what it does not mean (genetic determination, a statement about differences between groups or over time, or about the size of gene effects), and under what conditions an estimate is biased or changes.
cannot_establish: Any heritability figure for drug use or addiction (none is discussed), or how far the twin-design assumptions it describes hold for substance use disorders; its numerical examples are second-hand illustrations, quoted without intervals.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Numerical examples are taken from cited studies, for example IQ correlations summarized from 4,672 MZ and 5,546 DZ twin pairs (Box 4, p. 260).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; examples chosen by the authors to illustrate concepts.
sample.selection_effects: Examples were chosen to illustrate, mostly from agriculture, evolutionary biology and human height and IQ. 14 of the 115 references name one of the three authors as an author (editors' count), including the within-family marker method that the review presents as estimating heritability without the usual assumptions about family resemblance (p. 263).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (conceptual review). The review explains how heritability is estimated: offspring–parent regression, full- and half-sib correlations, the difference between MZ and DZ twin correlations, linear mixed ('animal') models fitted by residual maximum likelihood, Bayesian methods, and marker-based relatedness or identity-by-descent sharing (pp. 256–258, 263).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; the subject of the review is the parameter itself.
outcomes.operationalization: Heritability is defined as the proportion of total phenotypic variance in a population, for a measurement taken at a particular time or age, attributable to variation in additive genetic values (narrow sense, h²) or in all genetic values (broad sense, H²) (p. 255, Definitions; Box 1, p. 256).

analysis.effect_sizes: Illustrative values as cited (second-hand, without intervals): human height about 0.8 (Box 2, p. 257; p. 264), lowered to 0.6 if the 15-cm sex difference is not removed (p. 258); schizophrenia and major depression, with first-degree relative risks of 9 and 3 and incidences of 1% and 3%, heritabilities of 0.16 and 0.12 on the observed scale against 0.81 and 0.37 on the liability scale (p. 259); IQ twin correlations 0.86 (MZ) and 0.60 (DZ), twin-study estimates 0.5–0.8, and 0.3 (narrow sense) and 0.5 (broad sense) in a meta-analysis that modelled maternal effects (Box 4, p. 260); first-lactation milk yield in dairy cattle from about 25% in the 1970s to about 40% (p. 261); cricket wing dimorphism 0.71 in the laboratory and 0.21 in the field (p. 261); gene expression about 0.3 from MZ twins (p. 264). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (p. 259, approximate): human height in Finland about 0.82 for people born 1947–57 and about 0.72 for people born before 1929.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable; examples were chosen to illustrate.
analysis.power: The review notes that hundreds of observations are needed for a standard error of a heritability estimate below 0.1, and thousands for precise estimates (p. 258).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A conceptual account: heritability is a population- and time-specific ratio of variances that depends on the genetic and environmental variance present; it changes when either changes, when gene–environment correlation changes, with age, and with the method of measurement; a high value does not mean a trait is fixed by genes, says nothing about differences between groups or about changes in the mean over time, and says nothing about the number or size of gene effects; classical twin designs estimate only three variance components and rest on assumptions (equal shared environment for MZ and DZ twins, no gene–environment correlation) that bias heritability upward when they fail.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions present heritability as a key parameter for comparing the relative importance of genes and environment within and across populations, traits and environments (p. 255; p. 264); the conclusions also state its limits: it does not give the size of either variance component, refers to a particular population and environment and not to their differences, and tells nothing about individual genes (p. 264). The review says a heritability in one population does not in theory predict that of another but that in practice heritabilities of similar traits are often remarkably similar across populations and species (p. 256); a claim that heritability figures for addiction cannot be carried across populations needs both halves. Box 4 concludes from twin and family data that a large proportion of within-population IQ variation is associated with additive genetic factors while noting that some of the assumptions cannot be tested (p. 260). The expectation that marker-based within-family estimation will give unbiased heritabilities for contested traits (p. 263) is the authors' forecast for their own method.

timeline.event: Fisher parameterizes the resemblance between relatives; his percentages for human stature correspond to what are now called broad- and narrow-sense heritability (Box 3, p. 258).
Wright uses h for the path from genotype to phenotype; h² becomes the symbol for heritability (Box 3, p. 258).
Lush is thought to be the first to use the term heritability formally (Box 3, p. 258).

Visscher et al.: heritability of height estimated at 0.8 from genome-wide identity-by-descent sharing within sibling pairs, a method free of assumptions about family resemblance (as described, p. 263).

replication.where_it_stands: The review describes the statistical methods for estimating heritability as having more or less converged across species and disciplines while strong, often untestable assumptions remain for human behavioural traits (p. 255), and it lists open questions (why heritabilities have the values they do; why they change little under long selection; p. 264). Its expectation that marker-based methods would give estimates free of family-design assumptions bears on the DNA-based studies of substance use disorders on the same list (for example Hatoum et al. 2023), not read in this round.

funding.funder: Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (grants 389892, 442915 and 443011) and the Australian Research Council (grant DP0770096) (Acknowledgements, p. 266).
funding.declared_conflicts: No competing-interests statement in the PDF.
funding.affiliations_note: Queensland Institute of Medical Research, Brisbane (Visscher, Wray) and Institute of Evolutionary Biology, University of Edinburgh (Hill). Two of the authors' own papers are the marker-based estimation studies the review presents (refs. 56 and 62). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For drug use and addiction specifically: heritability estimates for substance use and substance use disorders made in the same population across birth cohorts and policy or availability regimes, on a stated scale (observed or liability), with designs that do not depend on the equal-environments assumption (adoption, within-family marker sharing), to show how far the figure moves when the environment changes.

domains.note: No search or criteria; examples were chosen by the authors to illustrate concepts.
Box 4 discusses the assumptions behind the IQ twin estimates, but other figures (schizophrenia and depression, milk yield, Finnish height, brain volume) are quoted without appraisal or intervals.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 14 of 115 references are the authors' own, including the marker-based method the review promotes as assumption-free.
Forecasts are marked as such (in the future, with sufficient data), and open questions are listed as unanswered.

domains.domain: Balance of views on the meaning and usefulness of heritability
domains.note: The sources the review cites for the nature–nurture controversy and for possible overestimation in twin studies (refs. 5, 90, 91 and 97, in Box 4) are named but their arguments are not set out; the review argues for the parameter's continued usefulness, so the critical side is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). For the site's purposes this is a conceptual explainer by specialists: its definitions and its list of what a heritability figure does and does not mean do not depend on a systematic search, and they are what claims should cite it for. Its numerical examples are second-hand, quoted without intervals, and two worked examples do not match the review's own formulas (see reporting issues). Cite it for definitions, misconceptions and the reasons heritability changes; do not cite its example figures as evidence about those traits, and do not cite it for any figure about drug use, which it does not discuss.

key_findings.finding: Heritability is defined as a ratio of variances: the proportion of total variance in a population, for a particular measurement taken at a particular time or age, attributable to variation in additive genetic values (narrow sense, h²) or total genetic values (broad sense, H²); it measures with one number the fraction of variation between individuals in a population that is due to their genotypes.

Because heritability is a ratio, numerator and denominator both matter: the denominator usually excludes variation due to known fixed effects such as sex, age and cohort; if the 15-cm average height difference between men and women were ignored, the heritability estimate for height would fall from 0.8 to 0.6.
key_findings.locator: Definitions, 2nd paragraph (p. 255); Estimation of heritability, 6th paragraph (p. 258, right column)

key_findings.finding: Heritability depends on the population: genetic variance depends on which alleles segregate, their frequencies, effect sizes and mode of action, and environmental variance also differs between populations, so in theory the heritability in one population does not predict that in another; in practice, heritabilities of similar traits are often remarkably similar across populations and even species. It can also differ between sexes and between early and late life (beef cattle: about 0.3 for weaning weight, 0.4 for market weight).

Misconceptions (Box 2): heritability is not the proportion of a phenotype passed on to the next generation (genes, not phenotypes, are passed on); a high heritability does not mean genetic determination, since the environment can change the phenotype (the secular rise in human height coexists with heritabilities of about 0.8), and for height (heritability 0.8, population SD about 7 cm) the SD of offspring around the parents' mean is 5.4 cm; a low heritability does not mean little additive genetic variance; heritability says nothing about the causes of differences between groups or of changes in the mean over time (Flynn effect; US-born white men about 9 cm taller than Dutch men in the mid-19th century, Dutch men now about 5 cm taller); a large heritability does not imply genes of large effect.

The usual partition of phenotypic variance assumes no gene–environment covariance and no gene-by-environment interaction; both are often ignored because they cannot be estimated, and according to the review, ignoring a covariance inflates the genetic variance, and ignoring an interaction inflates the environmental variance.

Estimation limits: the sampling variance of a heritability estimate is inversely proportional to the squared relationship of the relatives used and to the number of families, so hundreds of observations are needed for a standard error below 0.1; the classical twin design yields only three statistics (MZ resemblance, DZ resemblance, total variance), so only three variance components can be estimated although many more causes can be postulated; dominance and common-environment variance are confounded in full-sib designs; and resemblance partly due to common environment biases heritability upward.
key_findings.locator: Estimation of heritability, 4th and 5th paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: Heritability is not constant: it changes when genetic variance changes (selection, inbreeding, migration, mutation), when environmental variance changes, when the correlation between genes and environments changes, with age, and even with the method of measurement (self-reported against clinically measured height). Examples: first-lactation milk yield in dairy cattle from about 25% in the 1970s to about 40%; cricket wing dimorphism 0.71 in the laboratory and 0.21 in field cages (genetic correlation between the environments close to 1); livestock traits more heritable under good husbandry; the heritability of IQ rises with socio-economic status.
key_findings.locator: Heritability is not necessarily constant, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 summarizes heritabilities from reviews: on average larger for morphological than for fitness-related traits, and larger in better than in poorer environments; human height in Finland is shown for two birth cohorts, born 1947–57 (better environment) and before 1929 (poorer environment).
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the bar chart at 300 dpi against the axis ticks (approximate): about 0.82 for the 1947–57 cohort and about 0.72 for the pre-1929 cohort. The values are not printed.

key_findings.finding: For all-or-none traits such as disease, heritability depends on the scale: schizophrenia and major depression, with first-degree relative risks of 9 and 3 and incidences of 1% and 3%, have similar heritabilities on the observed 0/1 scale (0.16 and 0.12) but quite different ones on the underlying liability scale (0.81 and 0.37); heritability on the observed scale is always smaller than on the liability scale (at most 0.64, when incidence is 0.5 and liability heritability is 1), and for risk prediction from family history or genotypes the observed scale matters most.
key_findings.note: The pairs are not one worked conversion and do not follow from the Box 5 formula (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: IQ (Box 4): twin estimates are consistently 0.5–0.8 across ages (lower in preschool children, about 0.6–0.8 in old age); across many studies the average MZ and DZ correlations were 0.86 and 0.60 (4,672 MZ and 5,546 DZ pairs). Gene–environment correlation may inflate these estimates, and maternal (in utero) effects larger for MZ than DZ twins would bias them upward because equal common environments are assumed; a meta-analysis modelling maternal effects gave 0.3 (narrow sense) and 0.5 (broad sense). The box concludes that a large proportion of within-population IQ variation is associated with additive genetic factors.

Marker-based estimation within families: full sibs share on average 50% of their genome identical by descent with an SD of about 4% (half sibs 25%, SD 3%); relating this variation to phenotypic similarity gave a height heritability of 0.8, in line with twin and family studies, without assumptions about the causes of family resemblance; the authors expect such methods to allow unbiased estimation for contested traits such as IQ and for disease concordance.
key_findings.locator: Heritability in the genomics era › Exploiting variation in relatedness, 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: because heritability is a ratio of variances it does not give the size of either component; it refers to a particular population and environment and not to differences between them; and, as a composite measure, it tells nothing about the actions and interactions of individual genes.

How a trait is measured changes its heritability: the heritability of the mean of several records differs from that of a single record; with a single-record heritability of 0.10, the mean of 10 records has a heritability of about 0.53 when repeated measures share no environmental component, but only 0.125 when the correlation of repeated measures is 0.8.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with the formula that reproduces 0.53 gives 0.122 for the second case (see reporting issues).

reporting_issues.issue: Box 2 gives the SD of offspring height around the parents' mean as 5.4 cm, from a residual variance of 1 − ½h², whereas the Figure 2 legend gives residual variances about the offspring–midparent regression of 0.98 and 0.68 for h² of 0.2 and 0.8, which equal 1 − ½h⁴; by the editors' calculation the Figure 2 formula would give about 5.8 cm for height. The two describe spread around different quantities (the parents' genetic mean against their measured average), which the review does not distinguish.
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the point made (either value is close to the population SD of about 7 cm); cite the 5.4 cm figure as an illustration, not as a precise value.

reporting_issues.issue: In the repeated-measures example the review prints 0.125 for a repeatability of 0.8; by the editors' calculation, the formula that reproduces its first value (0.53, for a single-record heritability of 0.10 and no environmental repeatability), h²n/[1 + (n − 1)r] with n = 10, gives 0.122 for the second.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial rounding difference; no consequence for the claims.

reporting_issues.issue: The schizophrenia and depression example cannot be reproduced from the review's own Box 5 formula: by the editors' calculation, applying it to the printed liability-scale values (0.81 and 0.37) with incidences of 1% and 3% gives observed-scale values of about 0.06 for both, not 0.16 and 0.12. The printed observed-scale values equal 2K(λ − 1)/(1 − K) computed from the printed incidences and relative risks (0.162 and 0.124), and an exact liability-threshold calculation from the same inputs gives about 0.82 for schizophrenia but about 0.51 for depression. The review does not say how either pair was obtained; its note to ref. 19 calls the relationship approximate, while Box 5 states it as an equality.
reporting_issues.consequence: The qualitative point stands (for a rare disorder, observed-scale heritability is much smaller than liability-scale heritability), but the pairs should not be cited as a worked conversion, and Box 5's formula should not be used to convert published heritabilities of substance use disorders between scales.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 69 is garbled: its printed title repeats the opening of ref. 68's Arabidopsis title and ends with expression of PTGER4, while the text cites ref. 69 as a genome-wide association study of Crohn disease in humans.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 255–266: all 12 pages read on rendered pages at 150 dpi, including Boxes 1–6, Figures 1–2, references and acknowledgements; Figure 1 bars for Finnish height measured at 300 dpi against the axis ticks; worked examples recalculated in a scratch script; no supplement.
